Corporate events

Corporate event coordination for the person who has to run it

Conferences, awards nights, launches, offsites and staff celebrations. If the event has landed on your desk alongside your actual job, this page is about getting the brief right and someone competent to run it.

Get corporate event quotesEvent coordinators
  • Conferences, awards nights and launches
  • Briefs, run sheets and supplier management
  • Free to enquire

What does a corporate event coordinator do that an internal team cannot?

A corporate event coordinator carries the operational load that has no owner inside your organisation. Your marketing lead knows what the event is for and your executive assistant knows the diaries. Neither has three weeks to chase eleven suppliers and stand in a loading dock at six in the morning.

The work is supplier sourcing and quoting, venue negotiation, budget tracking, the run sheet, the briefing pack, on-site management and a reconciliation for finance. A corporate event organiser who has run your format also knows what goes wrong at an awards night at hour three. And when one external person owns the run sheet, everyone works from the same document.

Formats

Which corporate event are you running?

The format decides the lead time, the risk and the coordinator you want.

Conference

Sessions, speakers and delegates to register, feed and move between rooms. The longest lead time of any corporate format, six to nine months, and where a conference organiser or specialist conference planner earns their fee.

Awards night

A seated dinner with a live show attached. The run sheet is the whole product: award order, presenters, playback and a finish time that holds. Four to six months out.

Product or brand launch

Short, media facing and dependent on the space. Guest list, arrival and a hard finish. The fastest turnaround here, sometimes six to ten weeks, which raises the price.

Staff celebration or end of year party

Christmas parties, milestones and team nights. Book November and December six to nine months out.

Offsite or strategy day

Half venue, half running order. Rooms that suit workshops, catering that does not put everyone to sleep, and someone keeping time so the facilitator can focus.

Client or partner event

Smaller, relationship driven and judged on detail. Arrival, name badges, seating and food matter more than scale.

The brief

What your brief needs before anyone can quote it

Most quoting stalls for one reason: the brief is missing two or three things that change the price by thousands. Nobody can price around a gap.

The objective, in one sentence

Why the organisation is spending the money. Recognition, pipeline, retention, a launch, a thank you. A coordinator designs a different event for each.

Numbers and a date, confirmed

A firm minimum and a realistic maximum, because catering, AV and venue all key off them. Then the date, and whether it can move: a flexible window is often worth thousands in negotiation.

The approved budget, or at least the ceiling

Withholding the number gets you a proposal you have to reject, not a better price. Give the ceiling and say whether it excludes GST.

What has already been decided or booked

A venue held, an agency contracted, a speaker confirmed. Each narrows the scope and belongs in the brief, not in week three.

Your approval chain, its timing and its rules

Who signs off, how long they take, whether a board date has to be hit, and your compliance requirements: public liability cover, supplier onboarding and purchase orders. The thing most often left out.

Approval

How internal approval changes the timeline

A corporate event runs on two clocks: the event date and the approval process. The second surprises people.

01

Scope and sponsor first

Agree the objective, the size and who owns the budget before you contact a supplier. Approaching venues without a budget owner produces unusable quotes.

02

Brief, then quote

Write the brief, agree it internally, then release it. Sending different versions to different suppliers is why proposals cannot be compared.

03

Allow for onboarding, not just approval

Between choosing a supplier and paying one sits vendor onboarding, an insurance check, a contract and a purchase order, which takes two to four weeks.

04

Hold a contingency and name it

Venues and AV suppliers issue variations. Build one into the approved number rather than seeking a second approval in the final fortnight.

Deposits are the pinch point. Most venues will not hold a date without one and most approval processes will not release one quickly, which is how the date you thought you had disappears. Ask how long a venue holds a tentative booking and diarise the expiry.

On the day

The run sheet and the AV questions to settle early

The run sheet is what protects a corporate event. These are the AV questions that get expensive when asked late.

Room and AV items to settle before you sign a venue contract.
ItemThe question to askWhy it bites late
Screen and projectionWhat is in the room, at what resolution, and is it included?In house AV is often cheaper than hire but frequently mandatory, so it changes budget and supplier choice
MicrophonesHow many handheld, lapel and lectern mics are included, and is a technician required?Panels need more than anyone estimates, and extras are charged per unit on the day
Stage, lectern and seatingHow big is the stage, where does it sit, and how does the room seat your number?A stage in the wrong corner ruins sight lines for a third of the room
Video and audio playbackWho plays content, from what device, and are you recording?Audio from video is the most common technical failure, and adding a camera crew late changes the lighting
Power, cabling and internetWhat power is available where, and is there wired internet?Conference wifi that carries delegates rarely carries a live stream, and a wired line is ordered ahead
Bump in and rehearsal accessWhen can suppliers get in, and can you rehearse?A room in use until an hour before doors means no rehearsal and a set up in front of guests

Scroll the table sideways to see every column.

Your coordinator should circulate one version of the run sheet to the venue, the AV supplier, the caterer and your internal team. A run sheet in one inbox is not a run sheet. If the plan is built and you need only the day covered, on-the-day coordination is what to ask for.

Budget

What corporate event planning costs, and what moves it

Published Australian benchmarks for corporate work are thin. The one usable reference point is FAME Events, an Australian event agency, which in September 2024 described planning fees for non-wedding events as typically starting around $5,000 for a straightforward event. That is the fee only, not the event budget.

Four things move the fee. Guest numbers, because catering and staffing scale off them. Programme complexity, since an awards night with fourteen presenters is a different job from a cocktail function. Whether the venue is dry hire. And your timeline, since six weeks costs more than six months. Our planner cost guide sets out what the named Australian sources publish.

Quote on scope, not on a day rate

Ask every supplier to price the same scope: pre event hours, on site hours, site visits, how many people are on the ground and what a variation costs.

Separate the fee from event costs

Approvals go smoother when the coordination fee, the venue, the catering and the AV are separate lines.

Getting started

Finding a corporate coordinator in your city

Most coordinators cover a whole metropolitan market. If the event is interstate, ask what travel is charged. See event coordinators, event planning or venue sourcing.

Straight answers

Corporate event questions

What does a corporate event coordinator do?

They source and manage suppliers, negotiate the venue, track spend against your approved budget, write the run sheet, brief everyone working on the event, manage the day from bump in to pack down, and reconcile it for finance.

How far in advance should I book a corporate event coordinator?

Four to nine months for most formats, and six to nine for a conference or any function in November or December. Approval and vendor onboarding sit inside that window and take two to four weeks on their own.

What is the difference between a corporate event planner and a coordinator?

A corporate event planner builds the event from the objective: concept, format, venue, suppliers and budget. A corporate event coordinator takes a plan that exists, confirms it and runs it.

Do I need a conference organiser, or will a general coordinator do?

It depends on registration and speakers. If you are managing delegate registration, a speaker programme, concurrent sessions or ticketing, use a conference planner. A single stream day sits within a general coordinator's remit.

What do suppliers need before they can quote?

The objective, a firm minimum and maximum guest number, the date or range and whether it can move, the budget ceiling, anything already booked, and your approval chain. Send everyone the same brief.

Can a coordinator work with our existing suppliers and panel?

Yes, and in most organisations they have to. Many buyers have preferred venues, an AV partner or a procurement panel in place. Say so in the brief, and a corporate event organiser should work inside it.
